blocks.text: There's a thought many students have. It sounds like this:
"If my family had more money... if I could go to a better school… or something else then I could be successful too."
You think this is true, but it's not. It's just an imaginary story. And stories always change.
Most successful people didn't start from better places than you. They just decided to do something with what they had, by starting immediately to work on their dreams.
What most students think vs. what is actually true

rows: "People from big cities get more chances"

Most opportunities are on the internet ‘Today’.
Where you live matters Less, than ‘What you can do’.
"I don't have money to learn more"
‘YouTube, Google, Libraries, Conversations, are the best things that will ‘Change Your Life for Free’.
Research has shown that ‘Consistent Practice’ will lead to ‘Successful Outcomes’ rather than natural talent.

blocks.text: The pattern behind every success story
Every person who is successful has followed the same three steps.
Exposure → Effort → Consistency = Better Outcomes

Exposure means you come across something new - a field, a skill, a person, an idea, strategy, technique. It shows you something you didn't know before. This is why one of your tasks this week is to watch a video & get exposed. As ‘Exposure will help you Explore’.

Effort is the attempt you do, after you get the exposure. After watching the video you take notes, you ask questions, you compare & take small steps to ‘Evolve, Include, Verify, Introspect or Practice’.
Consistency means you are putting effort everyday to do the task until you Master.
Remember, you can't change your start, but you can choose well and ‘Control the End of Your Story’.
Most students think school is just something they have to do.
Go to class. Finish homework. Wait for the day to end, so they could enjoy themselves or be free.
This week's video lesson introduces a different way of seeing it: Your life is something YOU are creating.
Your School, family, friends, habits, and daily choices (through your perspective) are all part of that creation.
Strength vs Natural Gift
These are not the same thing.

rows:
A strength is something you become good at because you ‘Practice it’.
Examples:
Being hardworking
Being organised
Being good at maths after lots of practice
Note: Strengths can grow over time.

A natural gift is something that ‘Feels Easy for You’ but is difficult for others.
You did not learn it from anywhere.
Examples:
Making people feel comfortable
Explaining difficult things simply
Imagining and drawing your visualization
Solving complicated Science & Math problems
A natural gift usually feels ‘Fun to Work’, and normally when you do it, you ‘Forget about Time’. And you ‘Dont feel Stressed’

blocks.text: Which One Are You?

Imagine two kinds of farmers. Chemical Farmer and Organic Farmer that take care of the soil. Now imagine that you are the ‘Farmer of your career’ and look at steps a chemical & organic farmer would take.
Here is what that distinction looks like.

rows: "What do I need to understand better?"
You compare yourself to someone else
"I need to catch up fast to reach their level."
"I should focus on my own growth & talent and not compare."

blocks.text: Remember, The chemical farmer wants quick success. The organic farmer wants ‘real growth’.
Both put in effort,  but only one of them builds something that will last longer and ‘That is Legacy you should build for Life’.
Every student has two voices inside their mind.
One voice helps you do everyday things: Going to school, Finishing homework, Talking to people.
But there is another voice too. It says: "I'm not good at this." or "They are better than me."
This second kind of voice (Soch) impacts, inspires or affects your choices without you even noticing, that's called ‘Subconscious Influence’.
What Is Soch?
Soch means "thought."
But in this course, Soch means, ‘the way you see yourself and your life’.
Two students can sit in the same class, learn from the same teacher, and get different results.
But their Soch can still be very different, because of which, they may take different or opposite actions.

rows:
One student thinks:
"I need more practice. I can do better next time."

The other student thinks:
"I'm just bad at this subject, or the teacher isn't good"

blocks.text: Your Soch slowly grows from:
What people tell you again and again
Your past experiences
The things you tell yourself every day
The ideas, concepts, plans, opinions, thoughts, etc. you believe in
For example:

If someone fails once and thinks "I can never improve," that thought can become part of their Soch- subconscious influence, and dominate their further decisions and actions, and that thought can be dominated by fear.
But here is the important thing: Your Soch is not permanent. ‘It can Change’.
That is what this week's tasks will help you do.
Learning From A Role Model

Most students use role models in the wrong way. They only look at money, fame and success. Then they either feel excited for one day or discouraged because the gap feels too big. That influence does not help much. Here's how to learn from a role model correctly
Study Their Habits. Do not only look at their success. Look at what they did every day.
For example, Dhirubhai Ambani was known for listening carefully to all kinds of people.
Study Their Thinking (Soch) and Decisions. Look at how they handled problems & overcame them.
For example, Kalpana Chawla did not let her background decide what she could become.
This kind of thinking is something you can practise too depending on your need.
Remember, Your Soch shapes your subconscious influence and that shapes your actions. And remember your actions shape your future.
That is why this week is about noticing your thoughts, learning better ways to think, and practising them a little every day to ‘Evolve your Mindset and Identity’.
In the last three weeks, you learned what your strengths and natural gifts are, how your Soch (thoughts) affects your choices,  and how to learn from role models.
Now it is time to put everything together. This week, you will create your ‘Success Story’.
A Success Story is simply a clear picture of where you want to go and the kind of person you want to become, it’s not just about career but of life as a whole.
How to Build Your Success Story
A success story has three simple parts.
1. Where you are starting: This means your current situation. It includes your background, your family, your studies, and your present reality. Just write it honestly as it is.

2. What you are good at: This means your strengths and interests. Think about what you do well and what you enjoy doing. These signs can help you understand the direction you should move in, ‘It's okay’even if you do not know the exact career yet.
3. What you are working toward: This means your future goal. Imagine your life 10 years from now.
Think about the kind of life you want to live and what you want to be doing.
Vague vs. Specific What Makes a ‘Good Success Story’
A clear picture is more helpful than a vague one.

rows: Be Specific by asking ‘Questions’ to vague points.
How do I want to be successful?I want to become a teacher and help children learn with confidence

What kind of job do I want?
I want to be a software engineer who builds useful apps and sites.
I want to help my family.

How do I want to help my family? And Why?
I want to help my family by earning sufficient money. So my parents don‘t have to work any more and retire for the rest of their life.

blocks.text: The more clearly you can picture your future, the easier it becomes to work toward it.
Remember
Your Success Story does not have to be perfect. You can change it later.
The goal is to choose a direction and start moving.
Most students think confidence comes first. They wait and wait. They think: Once I feel ready, I will start.
But that is not how it works. Confidence builds because of the action.
The order is always this:
You Start a task → You finish it → You realise you could do it → You feel Better → That’s how confidence builds
Every time you do something, even if you do it badly, your brain gets a little proof. The next time, your brain says: I have done this before. Let me try, I can do it again.
That is building confidence.
The 1% Idea
1% means every time you sit down to work on something, try to do it just a little better than the last time. Even one small thing.

rows: What 1% Looks Like in Real Life
You try something new. It feels hard. That is normal.
You do it again. You stay five minutes longer than yesterday.
It feels a little easier today.

blocks.text: Day to day, you may not see the change. But after a few weeks, ‘You Will’.
How to Pick Your First Step
The most important rule is that your first step must be something you can do today, with no blocks in your soch (No money, no special preparation, no support).
For example:
Goal: Become a civil engineer.
Bad first step: Buy all the preparation books- This is acting directly before verifying
Good first step: Watch one YouTube video tonight about what a civil engineer does every day or read some article- This is verifying before acting.
The small step of verification is not the whole journey. It is just the first proof that you can begin.
Fear Is Normal. Everyone feels afraid sometimes. Even people you look up to.
The problem is what you do when fear shows up. Most students do one of two things:
They avoid it completely/ they just don't do that task or thing.
They think about it so much that it starts to feel even bigger and scarier that overwhelms them.
Both of these make fear grow. The only thing that makes fear smaller is doing something tiny but immediately, before the fear gets too big.
Common Fears at Your Age
Here are fears that most students feel:

rows:
Teacher judges me for a wrong answer
Class laughs when I speak up
I look stupid for asking a question, etc.

People judge what I say or do
People ignore me when I talk
People are rude to me
People don’t support, etc.

I will fail my exams, entrance.
I may disappoint my parents
I am not good enough compared to others
What if I don’t succeed

I end up alone
I make a mistake I cannot fix
Something bad happens again
I can’t express
How could I do it Alone

blocks.text: Look at the list again. Most of these fears are not happening right now. They are things you are imagining might happen. There is a big difference between the two (Imagination & Reality). The next section will show you why.
What Fear Tells You vs. What Actually Happens
This is the most useful thing to understand about fear, what you imagine will happen is always worse than what actually happens.

rows: Teacher responds normally or corrects your mistakes
Teacher answers, and others had the same question
They welcome and say Hi back

blocks.text: If Your Fear Comes from Something That Happened Before
Sometimes we are scared to try something because it went badly in the past. Maybe we failed, felt embarrassed, or got hurt.

But remember: that happened in the past. You have grown since then. You know more, and your situation may be different now. A bad experience from the past does not mean the same thing will happen again. It is just one part of your story, not the end of it. Control your Soch.
Communication Is Not Just Talking.  Most students think good communication means talking clearly. But there is more to it than that.
Good communication means two things:
Making the other person feel understood
saying what you mean in a way they can understand
The LUVR Method
Most people who have good conversations follow four simple steps consciously or subconsciously.

rows: Give your full attention when someone is speaking
Try ‘To Understand’ what they really mean, and ‘Not to just Reply immediately or judge’

blocks.text: For example: if your friend says, "I had a bad day," do not immediately start giving advice. First listen. Then try to understand why they are upset. You can ask, "Are you feeling sad because of what happened at school?" Once you understand, you can respond in a helpful way.
When we skip these steps, misunderstandings happen. But the good news is that there are some simple techniques anyone can learn.
5 Techniques to Communicate Better
1. The 2-second pause: When someone finishes speaking, wait for two seconds before you reply. This small pause helps you think about what they said instead of rushing to answer.
For example, when a teacher asks you a question, take a moment to think before speaking. Your answer will often be clearer and more accurate.
2. Ask better/ specific questions: If you are confused, ask a specific question.
Instead of saying, "I don't understand," try saying, "Can you explain that last part again?"
Specific questions help people understand exactly what you need help with.

3. Keep it short and clear: Try to speak in short and clear sentences. When we get nervous, we sometimes talk too much and miss our point. Simple words and short sentences make it easier for others to understand us.
4. Repeat back what you heard: Before you give your answer, say or reiterate what you understood in your own words.

This does two things. It makes sure you understand correctly. And it makes the other person feel truly heard, which is rare, and if you got it wrong people can correct you so you can then answer correctly.

5. Eye contact and expression: Communication is not only about words. People also notice your face, your eyes, and your body language. Try standing in front of a mirror and showing different emotions such as happiness, excitement, sadness, surprise, or kindness. This helps you understand how emotions look and feel. It also helps you express yourself more naturally when talking to others.
Remember

Good communication is a skill, just like playing a sport, drawing, or learning an instrument. People become better by practising in small everyday moments, with friends, family members, teachers, and classmates.

Many students face the same problem. They start the task with lots of excitement, energy and commitment, but after a few days, that excitement & energy fades away and commitment is withdrawn. This happens because of motivation
Motivation is a feeling, and feelings do not last forever. That is where discipline helps.
Discipline means doing what you planned to do, even when you do not feel like it or even when you feel lost or tired.

Imagine two students who decide to study for 30 minutes every day. One studies only when they feel motivated. The other studies every day at the same time, whether they feel motivated or not. After a few months, the second student will usually make much more progress.
The reason is simple: motivation helps you start, but discipline helps you keep going.
Your Personal Timetable
One of the best ways to build discipline is to have a simple daily routine/ timetable.
This template is for Day 1's task of building a timetable that fits your actual life. Fill in what works for your school timings, your family situation, and your daily commitments. Male it personal.

rows: Spend 15–30 minutes on your Personal Goal or Passion or Discipline
Read, reflect, keep the phone away

blocks.text: Once you create your timetable, keep it somewhere you can see it every day. A plan is much easier to follow when it is ‘right in front of you’.
Managing Distractions

One of the biggest challenges to discipline is distraction. Distractions can come from phones, television, games, notifications, friends, or even our own thoughts (Soch of fear, doubts, confusion, limitations, etc.). Instead of trying to fight distractions all the time, it is better to remove them before they become a problem.
For example:
Keep your phone in another room while studying.
Turn off notifications during study time.
Take a short walk, exercise if you feel stuck or restless before you focus on your studies or discipline.
Start with just a small task instead of waiting to feel ready for the ultimate goal.
Sometimes the hardest part is ‘simply getting started at once’.

Failure Is Not the End. Most students have been taught to avoid failure at home, at school, in front of relatives or in their regular life. A wrong answer in class feels embarrassing. Failing in front of others feels like proof that you are not good enough.

This week is about changing that idea (Soch) completely. Failure is not a sign that you are not good enough. It is a sign that tells you- there is something else you need to do, a sign to try differently, to understand that your current ways, techniques, strategies need to change.
What Failure Actually Is

Every skill you have today like- walking, writing, reading, speaking, communicating, studying, drawing, etc. was learnt through practice. You can agree that you made many mistakes while learning them.
You do not remember those failed moments as failure because no one was judging or grading you at that time.
Now that you are older, failure feels worse because you feel or know people are watching. But failure still works the same way. It is just information.

rows: "I should try again in a different or better way."

"Everyone makes mistakes while learning”
“No one will remember my mistakes once I succeed”

blocks.text: The students who improve the most are the students who learn from their mistakes and keep going.
How To Learn From Failure
Keep this process in front of you as you work through each day this week.
Step 1:  Try First: Do not spend too much time worrying about what might happen. Take the first step in 3..2..1.. and give it your best effort.
Step 2: Look At What Happened: Be neutral. Ask yourself: What went well? What was difficult? What mistake did I make? Be honest, but do not be harsh on yourself.

Step 3: Pick One Thing To Improve: Do not try to fix everything at once. Focus on one small part. Choose one small thing to work on. For example: Speak a little louder. Or  Practice one difficult question again.
Step 4:  Practise That One Thing: Spend a little time improving that specific skill. Small improvements are easier to notice and easier to align with further developments.
Step 5: Try Again: Give yourself another chance. Then ask: "Am I a little better than I was before?" If the answer is yes, you are making progress.
Reminder

Nobody becomes good at something on their first try. Every artist, athlete, teacher, doctor, engineer, and leader started as a beginner. They all made mistakes. They all had days when things did not go well.
What helped them grow was not being perfect. It was their ability to try again.
Self-Trust vs. Confidence

Many people think self-trust and self-confidence are the same thing, but they are different. Confidence is feeling sure that you can do something well. Self-trust is believing that you will keep trying, even when you are unsure or when there is no hope.

For example: You might not feel confident before a test, a speech, or a competition and that's ‘Okay’. But if you trust yourself for the practice and knowledge you have, you know that you will still show up, do your best, and learn from the experience if things go wrong.
That is why self-trust is so important. It helps you move forward even when confidence seems to be missing.
How to Build Self-Trust
Self-trust is simple: it is about keeping the promises you make to yourself.
Here are three ways to build it.

1. Keep Small Promises to Yourself: Choose one small task and complete it. The task does not need to be difficult. The important thing is that you would fulfil your commitment to yourself by doing what you said you would do. Because every time you keep a promise to yourself, your brain learns: I can trust myself.

2. Fix your breaks immediately: Everyone misses a day sometimes. That is normal.What matters is what you do next. If you miss one day of practice, Show up for yourself the next day. Do not wait for Monday or next week. Students who build self-trust are not perfect. They simply return to their habits quickly (May be Next Day) after that break and they don’t allow procrastinations, delays, laziness to take over their thoughts.

3. Do one thing nobody asked you to do: Do something toward your goal that nobody assigned, nobody will check, and nobody will reward.This is the most powerful level. Because the only reason you did it was your own decision. And when you repeat that enough times, it crafts your personality and makes you become who you desire to be.
Why We Avoid Things
Sometimes students avoid important tasks and say things like:
"I'll start tomorrow."
"I'm not ready yet."
"What if I fail?"
"I'll do it when I feel more confident."
Most of the time, the real problem is not a lack of time or ability. It is a lack of trust in themselves or to show up when you made a commitment to yourself.
They are just worried about making mistakes, and not actually doing well, or facing something difficult.
But self-trust grows when you take the first step, even when you feel unsure or low.
The question is not: "Am I ready?"
The better question is: "Can I trust myself enough to begin, Now?"
When students hear the word resilience, they often think it means being strong all the time and never feeling sad, tired, or frustrated. But that is not true.
Resilience means getting back up when you fall behind. It simply reflects the idea of coming back to your goal after you stop, you failed or you gave up for a while.
If you have been doing this course for 11 weeks, you have already shown resilience.  And this week is about building that skill even more ‘CONSCIOUSLY’.
The Three Stages of Learning

rows: Boring and repetitive backed by discipline
You are really building deepest skills at this stage with regular practice
Your hard work starts showing results

blocks.text: Some tasks this week will feel like the boring middle (stage 2). You will repeat the same thing. You will not see any change. But, we request you to do it anyway.
Because that is exactly where resilience is built.
Your Comeback Routine
At some point, you may miss a day or stop practicing for a while. That happens to everyone. The important thing is knowing how to start again. Follow the steps below to build your comeback routine.
Step 1: Say what happened in one sentence. You do not need a long explanation. Just something like: "I missed three days of practice because of exams and lost my momentum."
Step 2: Do not try to do everything at once. You’ll get overwhelmed and exhausted. It NEVER works. Just continue from where you stopped at the same task, same time and build on it 1 day at a time.
Step 3: Start small. If you usually practice for 20 minutes, start with 10 minutes. Doing a little is much better than doing nothing at all
Step 4: Focus only on today. Do not worry about the whole week or month. Just complete today's task.
Step 5: Tell yourself: "I came back today and finished my task." That one sentence is a sign of real resilience.
Resilience is one of the most important skills you can build that determines how far you go in your life.

Many students learn that the safest choice is always the best choice. This advice sounds smart, but it creates a problem. If you never try new things, you never grow or you never know your hidden potentials.
Think about the skills you built in this course. You spoke in front of others. You faced your fear. And you even practiced something that felt difficult.
Each time you did one of these things, you took a small calculated risk.
A calculated risk means taking a chance after thinking carefully about what could happen and deciding that you can handle the outcome.
The Calculated Risk Framework
Before you make an important choice this week, ask yourself these questions:
1. Best Case (Positive thought): What is the best thing that could happen?
2. Worst Case (Negative thought): What is the worst thing that could happen?
3. Most Likely Case (Neutral thought): What will probably actually happen?
Then ask one last question: Can I handle the worst case if it happens?
If the answer is Maybe, then trust yourself and take the step.  Many students discover that the worst case is not as scary as they first thought.
Calculated Risk vs. Reckless Choice
These are not the same thing. Confusing them leads to poor decisions.

rows:
You think before you act.
You verify the good and bad outcomes.
You know the possible downside.
You decide you can handle it.
You learn and improve after you try.

You act without thinking.
You ignore possible problems.
You jumped into it and regretted it later.
You ignore warning signs.
You give up after the initial failure

blocks.text: Reminder
You will never feel 100% certain before an important decision. Nobody does.
The students who move forward are the ones who ask the three questions, see that the worst case is something they can survive, and take the step anyway.
When something feels difficult, people usually think in one of two ways.
A fixed mindset says: Maybe I can't do this.
A growth mindset says: What can I learn to get better at this?
The situation is the same, but the way you think changes what you do next.
The Power of One Small Word: "Yet"
You can turn many negative thoughts into growth thoughts by adding one word: Yet

rows: I can't speak English confidently, Yet!
I'm not good at math, Yet!

blocks.text: The word "yet" reminds us that we can still learn and improve. It simply means: "I can't do it now, but I can learn."
The Same Situation, Two Different Responses

rows: "I need a better way to study."
"I need to try a different way."

blocks.text: One important thing is that a growth mindset does not mean you always feel positive. A growth mindset means you also stay curious to learn and adapt.
Instead of saying: "I can't do this."
You ask: "What can I do differently?"
Change the Method, Not Just the Effort
Sometimes students work harder, but they keep using the same method.
Students need to realise that if the method does not work, more effort may not help.
Sometimes you need a new approach.
Here are some examples:
If a topic feels confusing, try explaining it to a friend or family member.
If you forget what you read, stop and write one short sentence summary about it before moving on.
If you lose focus while studying, work for 20 minutes, take a 5-minute break, and then start again.

Last week, you learned about fixed and growth mindsets. This week, you will look at the beliefs behind those mindsets. Many students think they need more information to grow. Sometimes that is true. But often, old beliefs hold them back more than a lack of knowledge. These beliefs can affect what you try, what goals you set, and what you think you can achieve.
This week focuses on three steps:
1. Learn: Learn something new or build a new skill.
2. Unlearn: Let go of a belief that no longer helps you.
3. Relearn: Replace that old belief with a better and more helpful one.

Learning something new is often easy and relearning just takes practice. But letting go of an old belief is usually the hardest. Because many beliefs, especially limiting beliefs, doubts, fears, stay in our minds for years. We often treat them like facts, even when they are not true.
How to Spot a Limiting Belief
A limiting belief often sounds like a fact, which makes it hard to catch.
Ask yourself: "Is this a fact, or is it just something I believe is true?"

rows: This is a specific, real event
“People from small towns do not get big opportunities.”
People from villages, small towns can & have succeeded too

blocks.text: You can notice that the pattern is always the same.  Something happens. Then you create a story about it. After a while, the story starts to feel like a fact.
How to Create an Empowering Belief
An empowering belief does not mean that you tell yourself something that feels fake. It just needs to be honest and helpful.

rows: I can never speak confidently in public.
I need more practice. I can improve over time.
I always make mistakes under pressure.
I get nervous sometimes, but I can learn how to stay calm, take a pause, and apply the LUVR steps.
People like me do not get those opportunities.
If others can do it, I can find a way and do it too.

blocks.text: Reminder
You can let go of beliefs that hold you back and pick those thoughts (Soch) that help you believe in self and grow.
Working hard is important. But hard work alone is not enough. You also need to work in a smart way.
Students who improve the most do not always spend the most time working.They focus on the right things and use the right methods that help them learn better.
This week is not about working harder. You have already practiced that for the last 14 weeks.
This week is about asking: "Am I using the best way to learn and improve?"
What Smart Work Actually Means
Smart work does not mean doing less work. Smart work means using a good plan. You still need effort, but you also need the right method, strategies, techniques to help you upgrade to your next level.
Here is the practical difference:

rows: Reading the same notes again and again

You study for 90 minutes and test yourself on what you learned.
You discuss your issue with your teachers or siblings and find a way that can work for you.
You find your weak point (uncomfortable areas) and work on that specifically
Using the same method every time
You change the method when results stop improving. Discuss with your support group to find what can work for you and then unlearn and relearn.

blocks.text: Combining hard work with smart work is not easy. It is actually harder because it asks you to practice things you do not know yet. But that is exactly where real learning happens for you to upgrade to the next level.
The Four Questions
At the end of each practice session this week, ask yourself these questions to check whether you are combining hard and smart work.
1. What did I finish today? Think about what you actually completed. Be specific.
2. Did I do something challenging? If everything feels easy, you may not be learning much. A little challenge helps you to outgrow.
3. What did I learn today? If you can explain your outcomes or do your tasks better than before, you are making progress.
4. Is there a better way to do this? Sometimes a new method can help you learn faster or understand more. Do not be afraid to try a different approach.
Working hard is important. Working smart is important too. But when you combine both, you learn more, improve faster, and make better use of your time.

School teaches you many things through books, lessons, friends and teachers. But you can also learn from everyday life. You can learn by watching, listening, and paying attention to what happens around you.
This skill is called Observational Intelligence.
Observational intelligence means paying attention to the world around you and learning from what you see.
This week is about building that skill.
Four Signals the World Sends You
These four patterns show up in every person's life. Learning to read them is one of the most useful skills you can build.

1. Patterns: A pattern is when the same problem keeps coming back, even in different situations. When this happens, it can be a sign that you need to try a different approach or mindset. Example: You keep delaying your homework, then your practice, then a conversation you need to have. The topic changes but the behaviour stays the same.

2. Failures: Sometimes you try hard but still do not get the result you want. This usually means you are working on your goal through the wrong method. Failure is telling you to try a different way. Example: You study for a test but do not score well. You may need a different way to study.

3. Energy: Some activities make you feel excited and happy. Other activities make you feel tired. You have to pay attention to how different activities make you feel. This can help you learn more about yourself. Example:  You feel excited after drawing or playing football, but you feel tired after some other activities.

4. Feedback: People may notice things about you that you do not notice yourself. If several people tell you the same thing, listen carefully. Their feedback can help you improve. Example: If many people tell you that you explain things clearly, it could be one of your strengths.
How to Build Observational Intelligence
Like any skill, you can improve observation with practice. Here are four specific practices to build this skill.

Put Your Phone Away for Five Minutes: Sit quietly without your phone for five minutes. Look around you. Notice the People, Sounds, and Things happening around you. You’ll see things that you usually miss.
Look at Both Sides: When a problem happens, do not look at it from only your point of view. Ask yourself: "How would the other person see this?" This helps you understand situations Neutrally.

Listen Carefully: When someone talks to you, focus on what & how they are saying. Their use of words, language, tone and emotion. Do not think about your reply right away. Good listening helps you learn more about people.

Track Your Energy: For one week, notice how you feel after different activities. After each activity, write your feeling in one word: ‘Energized or Drained’. At the end of the week, look at your answers. You will discover activities that give you energy and activities that take energy away.
Sometimes the best lessons are already right in front of you.

Many students think stress is always bad. They try to avoid it, ignore it, or push through it. But stress is not always the enemy. Stress is a signal. Your mind and body use it to tell you that something needs attention.
The problem starts when:
You do not understand what stress means.
You ignore it for too long.
You let it control your actions.
This week, you will learn how to understand stress and respond to it in the right way.
Two Types of Stress

rows:
Good stress makes you feel nervous but ready. The important thing is ‘you can still focus’.
When it shows up
Before a test
Before a presentation
Before a competition
When you try something new
Good stress tells you that you care about something important.
It can help you prepare, focus, and do your best.

Bad stress makes you feel tired, overwhelmed, and unable to focus.
You may feel this:
When pressure lasts for a long long time
When fear, doubt or comparison takes over your thoughts
When you feel pain after not attempting
When you avoid meets, opportunities, interactions, tasks and be in that thought for a longtime
When you self talk through overthinking
Bad stress tells you that something needs to change. Your mind and body need rest, support, or a different approach.

blocks.text: You should deal with good stress and bad stress in different ways.
If you have good stress, break the task into small steps, get ready for the challenge and start working on it.
If you have bad stress, slow down for a while, reduce some of the pressure and take care of yourself before you try to fix the problem.
The: Identify → Classify → Respond Method
When you feel stressed, use these three simple steps.

Step 1: Identify: First, name the problem. Do not just say, "I feel stressed." Try to be specific. For example: "I feel stressed because my test is in four days and I still need to study three chapters." When you name the problem, it becomes easier to understand and take steps to solve the issue.

Step 2: Classify: Next, ask yourself: "Is this good stress or bad stress?" Good stress comes from a challenge that you can prepare for and overcome. Bad stress comes from pressure that has built up for too long and is making it hard for you to cope or have hope in the outcome and belief in self.
Step 3: Respond: Now choose the right response.
If it is good stress: break the task into small steps, start with one small step right away and focus on what you can do next.
If it is bad stress: talk to someone you trust, take a short walk or do some stretching or let go off that target for sometime and take proper rest and give yourself time to recover.
Remember
Stress is not always a problem when you understand it and respond in the right way, you can handle it much better and convert that stress into energy and push for your real growth.
Every day, you feel different emotions.

Sometimes you feel happy.  Sometimes you feel negative emotions like- being nervous, angry, frustrated, or disappointed, and sometimes you feel positive emotions like- being happy, blessed, satisfied, proud or a winner
You cannot stop these feelings from appearing. But you can choose what you do next.
Emotional intelligence is the skill of understanding your feelings and responding in a helpful way instead of reacting without thinking.
This skill helps you make better decisions, solve problems, and build stronger relationships.
The ACER Framework
You can build emotional intelligence by using the ACER Framework.

A – Awareness: Awareness means noticing and naming your feelings. Instead of saying, "I feel bad," try to be more specific. For example: "I feel nervous because I have a test tomorrow and I have not finished studying." When you name the feeling clearly, you can understand the problem more easily and that you don't name yourself with that temporary feeling.

C – Control: Control does not mean hiding your emotions. It means you do not let your emotions control your actions & decisions. You feel angry, but you don't react in anger rather you choose kind words. You feel nervous, but you still try. You feel frustrated, but you keep working.
The breathing technique from Week 17 helps here. Take a slow breath when your emotions feel strong.
Breathe in for 4 seconds. Breathe out for 6 seconds. This simple habit can help you stay calm and think clearly.
Or You can also take a pause for a moment to align your mind before you take any further step that can never be reversed or deleted.

E – Empathy: Empathy means trying to understand how other people feel. For example, a friend may seem upset, quiet, or angry. Instead of judging them, ask yourself: "What might they be going through?" Empathy helps you become a better friend, teammate, and family member. It also helps you understand your own feelings better.

R – Response: Every emotion gives you information. Your response is what you choose to do next. A reaction happens automatically. A response is a choice but a wise one. When you pause and think before you act, you make better decisions, relations and emotions for yourself.
The more you practise this framework the better you become at understanding your emotions and making good choices.

Sometimes things do not go as planned. Sometimes a study plan does not work, a challenge takes longer than we thought or a problem gets in our way. When this happens, adaptability helps you keep moving forward instead of giving up.

Adaptability means changing your plan when you need to while still working toward the same goal. The goal stays the same, but the path can change, your steps can reverse and you can relearn after unlearning.
Think about a river. When a rock blocks its way, the river does not stop flowing. It finds another path around the rock and continues moving forward. You can do the same.
This week is about learning how to adapt when things change or don’t go as planned.
The Octopus: Three Techniques for Adapting
The octopus is one of the most adaptable animals in the ocean. It can handle change very well and find ways around problems. We can learn a lot from the way it responds to challenges.
Here are three simple lessons we can learn from the octopus.
Technique 1:  Colour Change: Read the new situation first.
When an octopus enters a new place, it does not act right away. It looks around first. It notices what is happening and then decides what to do.
You can do the same. Sometimes things do not go the way you expected. Maybe you get a lower mark than you hoped for. Maybe a friend says something that upsets you. Maybe your plan does not work.
Before you react, stop and take a moment to understand the situation. Think about what happened and what you can do next, rather than react to that situation.
Technique 2: Ink Release: Create space to think.
When an octopus feels danger, it releases ink. The ink gives it time to move away and think clearly.

You can do the same when a problem feels too big or confusing. You do not have to solve everything immediately. Give yourself a little time to think. A short pause can help you see the situation more clearly and make a better choice. Allow yourself to take a break when things seem blurry or confusing.
Technique 3:  Body Squeezing: Find the unexpected path.
The octopus can fit through small openings. When one path does not work, it looks for another one.
You can do that too. If your first plan fails, do not stop. Ask yourself:
What else can I try?
Is there another way to solve this?
Any support group people who can help?
Any reflections from the local or global role models?
Would I ask a friend to do it?
Remember
Being adaptable does not mean being aimless. Your goal and your values do not change. What changes is how you get there. The route, the method, the timeline all of these can change when they need to.

You are just about to complete 20 weeks i.e. 5 months. Think about that for a moment. Weeks ago, you started this journey. You wrote about your goals, your challenges, and the things you wanted to improve.

At that time, you did not know what the course would be like. But you kept going. You might have missed some days. Some weeks might have felt easier than others. But Kudos to you, you came back and continued, never gave up, trusted the process and pushed yourself.
That is what this week is about: Consistency.
What Consistency Actually Is

Consistency does not mean doing the work when you feel motivated. Motivation comes and goes. You cannot build a daily habit on it. Think of it this way: Motivation is like rain. Rain helps plants grow, but it does not rain every day. A farmer cannot wait for rain before taking care of the farm. That is why farmers water their plants regularly.
In the same way, you cannot wait to feel motivated before doing your work. You need to keep showing up, even on days when motivation is missing, you are at your lowest.
Here is the exact difference:

rows: You practise when you feel inspired
You practise at the same time every day, No Matter What
You skip when you are tired
You fulfil your commitment even on days when you are tired or exhausted
You stop when you cannot see results
You continue because you know results come after constant work for a long time

blocks.text: What Stops Consistency and What to Do About It
Everyone finds it hard to stay consistent many times. The important thing is to know what gets in your way and learn how to handle it.

Low energy:  Some days you may not feel like doing the task. That is normal. Start with a small step. Even five or ten minutes of effort is better than doing nothing. But do it with total consistency and consciousness.

A bad practice session: Not every practice session will go well. That does not mean today's session was a waste. The most important thing is not to have the idea of having a perfect session, rather your target should be to show up and do the same old thing irrespective it gets boring and dull.

Routine Changes: Holidays, family events, and busy days can make it harder to follow your usual routine. On those days, do a smaller version of the habit. A little progress is still progress. You just need to be committed to what you desire to build or become.
Slow Progress: Sometimes it may feel like you are not improving. But many good things take time. Keep showing up and keep practising. The results will come if you stay consistent.
Most students have been asked the question multiple times: "What do you want to become when you grow up?"
Many people answer with a job title. Doctor. Engineer. Teacher. Designer, etc.

But choosing a career is not just about picking a job from a list. Before you decide what you want to become, you need to understand who you are. Beacuse the best career is the one that fits your strengths, interests, and values, not the most impressive or famous one.
This week is about discovering that ‘Fit’.
How to Find a Career That Fits You

Many students start by looking at different careers. They think about what pays well or what other people suggest. Then they try to fit themselves into one of those careers. That isn’t the right way or This is the most incorrect way to select a career. Try a different approach. Start with yourself first. Understand who you are, and then look for careers that match your personality, preferences, interests, likes & dislikes, natural potential and talents.
Ask yourself these three questions to find the best fit:
1. What comes Naturally to you? Think about the things you do easily. These are often the things that feel simple to you but difficult to other people.
2. What do you Keep Coming Back To? Think about the topics, activities, or hobbies that interest you again and again. Long-term interests and participation often tell you a lot about yourself.

3. What kind of Impact or Difference do you want to make? Do you want to teach people, help people, create things, solve problems, organise tasks, lead or any other task? Your answer can help you find careers that feel meaningful to you.
From Interests to Careers
Sometimes you know what you enjoy, but you do not know what careers, jobs or opportunities connect to it. Here are some examples:

rows: Types of Careers You Can Relate To
Teaching, content creation, journalism, sales, marketing, advertising
Finance, accounting, data analysis, engineering, banking, insurance, mathematician, economist
Counselling, healthcare, social work, human resources,
Event management, project management, business operations, hospitality, business management
Design, architecture, film, advertising, fashion, interiors, fine arts, product, jewellery

blocks.text: Remember

The goal is not to choose a career today. The goal is to understand yourself better with a variety of choices that  connect with your core and soul, so you can make better & informed choices in the future.
Many students know what they want in the future. They might want a career they enjoy or a successful life. But many students do not know what they need to do today to reach those goals.
A five-year plan helps connect your future goals to the actions you take now. Your plan does not have to be perfect. Some things will change over time. That is Normal.
The purpose of a five-year plan is not to predict the future. It is to give you a clear direction and help you take the right steps today.
How to Set Goals That Work
Some goals sound good but do not tell you what to do.

rows: Practise English for 15 minutes every day
Study my weakest subject for 30 minutes each day
Complete my daily habit for 30 days, no matter what

blocks.text: A clear goal tells you exactly what action to take. When you know what to do, it becomes easier to get started.
Your Three Checkpoints
A five-year plan works best when you break it into three steps. Each step builds on the one before it.

rows:
This is the starting point. You focus on building habits and basic skills. You also complete small but important goals.
Example: Study regularly, improve weak subjects, build a daily routine, and start learning skills related to your interest.

This is the growing stage. You start moving closer to your chosen field/goal. You get more real experience and exposure.
Example: Join internships, training, workshops, or projects. Start exploring your career area more seriously.

This is where you start seeing major progress. You begin real work or take your first step into your career.
Example: Get a degree, job, or professional path related to your goal. Start applying your skills in real situations.

blocks.text: Each step depends on the one before it. You cannot reach Year 3 without Year 1, and you cannot reach Year 5 without Year 3.
Remember

You do not build your future in one day. You build it through small actions fulfilled daily, good habits, and useful skills. Focus on what you can do today, and let those small steps lead you toward your bigger goals.
22 weeks ago, you started this journey as a student who was, ‘Lost, Unaware, Unsure or Unclear’ of how to proceed towards a successful career. But you are not that person anymore.
In these 22 weeks, you have worked on yourself step by step. You did not wait for perfect conditions or the perfect environment. But you kept learning even on difficult days.
This week is not about learning something new. It is about noticing how much you have already learned and planning to use it all at once in a single plan.
What “Becoming Successful Anywhere” Means
This week’s title is not about becoming famous or reaching one fixed goal. It means something simple and practical. It means your strength is not outside, but it is inside you.
We all can do well when everything around us is perfect. Good teachers, good support, and easy conditions. When things change, we may find it hard to continue and impact similarly.

But now we all will have to craft a mindset of who can do well even when things are difficult. We can adjust, learn, and keep going in any given situation. This happens because we have built strong skills like discipline, confidence, emotional control, communication, adaptability and a lot more that only we can justify for ourself
That is the kind of individual this course has been helping you become.
The Only Thing Left

Everything you have learned in this course has helped you build important skills like confidence, discipline, observance, communication, emotional control, risk taking, adaptability, and a clear direction for your future.
Now these skills are with you. What is left is simple: you need to use them.
Every day, you can make small choices like:
Show up and work on your Year 1 goals, even if you do not feel ready
Do not let one bad week stop your progress
Keep moving in your chosen direction, even if results are not clear yet
Learn from mistakes instead of giving up
Trust the effort you have put in over the last 23 weeks
The distance between where you are now and where you want to be is about taking small, steady actions every day.

For the last 23 weeks, you have worked on yourself and learnt things you never knew were hidden within you.. You explored your strengths, interests, likes, dislikes, habits, thoughts, mindset, confidence, communication, discipline, adaptability, purpose, vision and goals. Through them you crafted a different version of yourself
Now comes the most important part. You know the process of moving from your current self towards your  future self and the only thing you have to follow to upgrade is Use all of it at once.
Think of your journey like this:
KNOW → CHOOSE → BUILD → ACT → LEARN → IMPROVE → GROW

blocks.text: This table guided above is not a one-time process. You can use it again and again, regularly and throughout your life. You can apply it to your daily choices, academics, career, routines, habits,  mindsets, beliefs, decisions, actions, relationships and life as a whole.
But most importantly this is not a standard, rather this is an idea and you can alter it based on your experiences and what you need at different stages of life.
But you can always come back to the same process to reflect and get the right support to make the right difference.
One Last Responsibility
Your success is not only about you. If you get support from your family, friends, teachers, role models, or this course, remember that support. One day, someone else may need the same support.
Be that person for them.
If you see someone with talent, curiosity, or a dream, encourage them. If you can help, do help someone else find their meaning and purpose of life.
And while you build your own future, take care of the world around you too.
Keep your surroundings clean.
Protect Nature–as Nature needs humans the most.
Use resources carefully.
Do what you can to make the future better.
Be the ‘Best You’ that can be proud of yourself by the end of the day!
